citations.quote: Even when based on standard methodologies, the reuse of model elements remains cumbersome and error-prone, leading to risks of inconsistent traceability and functional misalignment across missions. Moreover, existing agile functional modeling approaches are not always aligned with broader digital transformation goals, as they typically rely on graphical notations, which limit model accessibility and make reuse complex and time-consuming.

Therefore, this paper proposes an object-oriented functional approach for managing satellite platform digitalization in a modular and reusable manner through functional grouping. An automated framework was developed to support fast, consistent deployment of satellite digital models across missions, leveraging standard solutions and use cases.

The satellite provider owns standardized satellite platforms, proven across multiple missions, to chose from to match customer's mission and payload requirements in terms of mass and volume, required pointing accuracy, propulsion needs, downlink data rate, interface compatibility, orbital constraints, and power consumption [5].
A System as Code practice allows for an agile system development with automated workflow and configuration management of the digital thread, leveraging model patterns and reference models.

This work addresses that gap by proposing an automated object-oriented functional modeling approach, enabling faster and more consistent generation of functional architectures based on known solutions provided by satellite platform suppliers. The approach is tailored to the modular and service-oriented context of the New Space sector and supports configuration management across varying mission scenarios.

Spacecrafts are typically composed of recurring functional subsystems, such as propulsion, attitude determination and control, communications, command and data handling, thermal control, power supply, and structures and mechanisms, that can be modeled using MBSE to promote interface standardization, subsystem reuse, and traceable system decomposition.

In this paper, a tailored application of the ARCADIA methodology is presented, incorporating key concepts from the FAS methodologies, which is typically implemented within SysML-based modeling tool. ARCADIA was selected because of the coding integration capabilities given by the Python4Capella add-on [27]. It allows the study of System as Code transition potential. The proposed approach is first applied using a conventional modeling process, and then extended with automating capabilities given by Python4Capella.

The model begins at the Operational Analysis (OA) level, defining the overall space program context and mission objectives. The functional analysis is conducted primarily within the System Analysis (SA) and Logical Architecture (LA) layers, where needed system functions and functional decomposition are captured and structured. Finally, the Physical Architecture (PA) addresses the concrete selection of hardware and software elements to realize the logical components.
For this research, the satellite platform was chosen as the primary SoI, aligning with the practical needs of the New Space industry while allowing future extension to broader system elements.

A key concept from the FAS methodology adopted in this work, applied in conjunction with the ARCADIA methodology and illustrated in Fig. 2, is the principle of rigorous functional grouping based on use cases, which reflects OOP principles of abstraction and encapsulation. This approach strengthens traceability between stakeholder needs and system functionality, and forms the foundation for a modular and reusable MBSE framework adapted to the challenges of the New Space Economy.

In New Space organizations, multiple baselines are often available, each representing a pre-validated logical architecture reused from previous missions. Based on the best alignment with customer requirements, the most appropriate baseline can be imported into the current model and extended to accommodate mission-specific elements.

This modeling flexibility allows the architecture and function tree to be tailored to the specific interests of different engineering disciplines, enabling the accurate representation of system-specific features at the appropriate level of abstraction.

The native solution of ARCADIA to re-use elements across multiple projects is the Capella Replicable Element Collection - Replicas (REC-RPL) combined with specific Capella projects defined as Libraries. This strategy let the user copy and paste manually elements from a project to another. To deepen model interaction capabilities, the Python4Capella addon was considered. Python scripts are used to to read and write from/to the Capella model.

Main Automation Script is used to deploy the automation program within Capella. It is divided into two sections: a declarative section, where standard functional libraries are imported via their associated Python classes, and an execution section, where the actual mission model is assembled by instantiating and configuring predefined functional groups.

To enable this capability, the first step was the development of a User-Defined API layer, which provides an adequate mapping between Python and Eclipse Java classes for Capella model elements not covered by the given Capella Simplified API.

For each capability relevant to satellite development, a dedicated functional library is created, structured in two sections: one for functions and components, the other for functional and component exchanges.

In summary, it becomes possible to retrieve the functional analysis library by calling the corresponding Python class, which encapsulates the necessary logic and structural definitions. As a result, the model, spanning both the System Analysis and Logical Architecture layers, can be automatically generated and validated.

For instance, adding a power-demanding component triggers the Provide Power capability, linking it to the Power Conditioning and Distribution Unit (PCDU), and informing decisions on electronics layout and cable routing.

Through Python4Capella, it becomes possible to dynamically access and update model elements, enabling bidirectional integration with external data sources and simulation environments. This requires models to be populated in a structured format to support automation and repeatable data flows [6].

The validation of the automating architecture was performed through manual inspection of the resulting model, ensuring that automation produced the correct elements without omissions or unintended artifacts, and through Capella's built-in model validation tools. Functional libraries were also tested, and iteratively refined, including validation of interconnections both within and across groups. These checks were carried out incrementally, starting from individual model elements and scaling up to complete functional group implementations. This dual approach confirmed both the semantic correctness and structural consistency of the automated workflow, forming the basis for the conclusions presented in the following section.

An automated object-oriented systems engineering approach, combining modular functional groups derived from use cases, has proven effective in enhancing model modularity, traceability, and replicability in the context of the New Space scenario. While the initial modeling effort is higher, particularly during the transition to a System as Code framework, the benefits in terms of faster model deployment and consistent reusability outweigh the short-term cost.

However, limitations were observed in the maintainability of the custom automation layer, which is deployed across multiple custom APIs and Python classes, and therefore requires disciplined management. Manually constructing the functional libraries presents limitations in terms of scalability and maintainability. Their initialization, particularly with respect to functional interfaces, through scriptable APIs from a dedicated model is therefore essential to ensure robustness and reduce both implementation time and error.

The structure of the functional libraries used in the automated implementation process with Capella includes essential attributes for both functions and exchanges. For each function, the library defines its name, parent function, kind, and implementation case, which determines how it is treated during generation (e.g., as an abstract or leaf element). Each function is also associated with a component and parent component, along with a cardinality value indicating whether multiple instances are required. An inclusion field specifies dependencies on other capabilities. For functional exchanges, the library records the exchange name, source and target functions, owning function, exchange category, implementation case, and linked component exchange.

The mapping of model elements must be performed using the Capella element IDs, which are assigned only after model generation. As a result, this information cannot be pre-defined or included directly in the functional library. Instead, it must be accounted for during any subsequent manipulation or access to the model via the Python4Capella API.

A key aspect of this approach is to create a base that facilitates the accessibility of model information to multidisciplinary engineering teams, with a digital thread framework and automated reporting pipelines.

The baseline satellite platform was modeled in Capella in a modular manner aligned with established design heritage and digital thread integration needs. Functional decomposition followed object-oriented principles, where use case driven functional groupings were implemented and refined using inheritance structures and abstract definitions. Functional libraries were built upon the functional groups.
